title: GitLab Overview
summary: GitLab is a DevSecOps platform that helps teams plan, build, secure, and deliver software through connected workflows.
employeeUseCase: Candidates can describe GitLab as both a product company and an operating model: a DevSecOps platform supported by transparent, handbook-first ways of working.
highlights: GitLab brings software planning, source code, CI/CD, security, and delivery workflows into a connected platform.
The public handbook explains how GitLab operates internally, including remote work, communication, values, and decision-making.
The Direction material explains how GitLab thinks about product strategy and the DevSecOps lifecycle.

title: GitLab Handbook
summary: the handbook is GitLab's public operating manual for company policies, processes, values, and team practices.
employeeUseCase: Employees and candidates can use the handbook to self-serve context before asking for help, making onboarding and cross-functional work faster.
highlights: The handbook acts as a single source of truth for how GitLab works.
Public documentation supports transparency, asynchronous work, and repeatable onboarding.
Handbook-first habits reduce repeated explanations and help people audit decisions later.

title: GitLab Values
summary: GitLab's values translate culture into practical behaviors: collaboration, results, efficiency, diversity-inclusion-belonging, iteration, and transparency.
employeeUseCase: A new employee can use the values page to understand what good judgment looks like in daily work, not only in performance reviews.
highlights: Values are written as behaviors that employees can apply in real situations.
Transparency and iteration reinforce GitLab's public, handbook-first operating model.
The values are useful for candidates because they reveal how GitLab expects people to make tradeoffs.

title: Transparency
summary: transparency at GitLab means sharing information broadly by default, documenting decisions, and making work visible while respecting sensitive information.
employeeUseCase: Employees can reduce confusion by moving decisions, rationale, and status updates into visible artifacts that others can inspect asynchronously.
highlights: Transparency gives people access to context they need for better decisions.
Public artifacts make it easier for candidates, customers, and employees to learn how GitLab thinks.
Transparency still requires guardrails for confidential, personal, legal, security, or customer-sensitive information.

title: Iteration
summary: iteration encourages small, meaningful improvements shipped quickly, with feedback used to make the next change better.
employeeUseCase: Employees can use iteration to reduce risk: ship the smallest useful improvement, invite feedback, and keep moving.
highlights: Iteration favors progress through small changes over waiting for a perfect large release.
Small changes help teams learn faster and lower the risk of each individual decision.
Iteration is especially useful when the full answer is not known yet.

title: Collaboration
summary: collaboration at GitLab is about helping others succeed through shared context, kindness, direct communication, and cross-functional work.
employeeUseCase: A candidate can show culture fit by explaining how they make work easier for teammates across functions and time zones.
highlights: Collaboration is easier when expectations and context are documented.
Direct communication and kindness can coexist in high-performing teams.
Cross-functional work improves when people make ownership and next steps explicit.

title: Results
summary: results emphasizes measurable outcomes, customer value, ownership, and prioritizing work that moves important goals forward.
employeeUseCase: Employees can connect project updates to outcomes instead of activity, which is important in remote and asynchronous environments.
highlights: Results-oriented communication focuses on outcomes, not performative busyness.
Clear ownership helps distributed teams understand who is driving a decision or deliverable.
Customer value is a useful lens for prioritizing tradeoffs.

title: Efficiency
summary: efficiency encourages boring solutions, reducing waste, making good tradeoffs, and using time deliberately.
employeeUseCase: Employees can use efficiency to choose simple, maintainable solutions and avoid unnecessary process overhead.
highlights: Efficiency is about using time and attention deliberately.
Simple solutions are often better than complex systems that are hard to maintain.
Async documentation can be more efficient than repeated synchronous explanations.

title: All-Remote Work
summary: GitLab describes all-remote work as an intentional operating model built on documentation, asynchronous communication, clear ownership, and trust.
employeeUseCase: Remote employees can stay effective by documenting decisions, writing with context, and avoiding unnecessary synchronous dependency chains.
highlights: Remote work succeeds when information is written down and available without needing a meeting.
Asynchronous practices let teams collaborate across time zones while preserving focus time.
Clear ownership and documented decisions reduce ambiguity for distributed teams.

title: Asynchronous Communication
summary: GitLab handles asynchronous work by making written communication, documented decisions, clear ownership, and low-context updates the default way teams coordinate.
employeeUseCase: Employees should write updates so someone in another time zone can understand the context, decision, owner, and next step without needing a live meeting.
highlights: Async work depends on writing things down before asking for synchronous time.
Good async updates include enough context for people who were not in the original conversation.
Documented decisions make it easier for distributed teams to move forward without waiting on meetings.

title: Communication
summary: GitLab's communication guidance emphasizes low-context writing, asynchronous updates, and making decisions discoverable.
employeeUseCase: Employees can reduce meetings by writing updates that include context, decision history, owners, and next steps.
highlights: Low-context communication helps people understand decisions without private background knowledge.
Async updates are preferred when a real-time meeting is not necessary.
Writing down decisions supports transparency and helps future teammates understand why choices were made.

title: Meetings
summary: GitLab's meeting guidance favors intentional synchronous time, clear agendas, documented outcomes, and asynchronous alternatives when possible.
employeeUseCase: Before scheduling a meeting, employees can ask whether a written update, merge request, issue, or decision record would be more effective.
highlights: Meetings should have a clear purpose and documented outcome.
Async communication is preferred when a meeting is not necessary.
Reducing unnecessary meetings preserves maker time across distributed teams.

title: Decision-Making and DRIs
summary: GitLab decision-making works best when ownership is clear, context is documented, and the directly responsible individual drives the next step.
employeeUseCase: Employees can make progress faster by naming the owner, writing the decision context, and recording the outcome where others can find it.
highlights: Clear ownership prevents distributed teams from waiting on ambiguous consensus.
Decision records help future teammates understand why a choice was made.
The DRI concept supports accountability while still inviting input from collaborators.

title: Onboarding and Self-Service Learning
summary: GitLab onboarding relies on public documentation, self-service learning, clear expectations, and repeatable processes that help new team members ramp quickly.
employeeUseCase: A new hire should use the handbook to learn operating norms, find owners, understand values, and reduce repeated questions during ramp-up.
highlights: Handbook-first onboarding gives new team members access to context before they need to ask someone live.
Repeatable onboarding improves consistency across locations and time zones.
Self-service documentation helps candidates understand how GitLab works before joining.

title: Handbook-First Work
summary: Handbook-first work means documenting processes, decisions, and operating norms in a shared source of truth before relying on private conversations.
employeeUseCase: Employees should update the handbook or a durable artifact when they discover repeated questions, unclear process, or decisions that others will need later.
highlights: A handbook-first habit turns repeated explanations into reusable documentation.
Durable written artifacts support transparency and async collaboration.
When the handbook is outdated, the better behavior is to improve it rather than route around it.

title: Merge Requests and Code Review
summary: GitLab merge requests are collaboration spaces where implementation, review, discussion, and decision context stay close to the code change.
employeeUseCase: Engineers can use merge requests to make work visible, invite feedback, document tradeoffs, and connect code review to the broader DevSecOps workflow.
highlights: Merge requests support transparent collaboration around code changes.
Good code review improves quality while preserving context near the implementation.
MR workflows connect planning, source code, review, CI, and delivery.

title: Merge Request Reviewers
summary: GitLab merge requests can have reviewers: people requested to review proposed changes before the work is merged.
employeeUseCase: A developer who opens a merge request can add or change reviewers from the merge request page/sidebar so the right people are asked to review the change.
highlights: Reviewers are used to request code review on a merge request.
The Reviewers field or sidebar keeps review ownership visible on the merge request.
Reviewers and approvals are related but not identical; approval rules can be configured separately.
Adding reviewers helps route feedback while keeping discussion, implementation context, and decisions near the code change.

title: Comments and Discussions
summary: In GitLab, a comment is a note or discussion message attached to work such as an issue, merge request, commit, or snippet so people can ask questions, give feedback, mention teammates, and keep collaboration connected to the work item.
employeeUseCase: A beginner can think of comments as the conversation layer in GitLab: use them to ask for clarification, leave implementation feedback, reply in threads, mention teammates with @username, and record context where the work is happening.
highlights: Comments help keep questions and decisions connected to the issue, merge request, commit, or snippet they are about.
Discussions and threads separate different feedback items so conversations are easier to follow.
Mentions can bring specific teammates into a conversation when their input is needed.
Resolvable discussions help teams show when feedback has been addressed.

title: Merge Request Comments and Discussions
summary: GitLab merge requests support comments and threaded discussions so people can ask questions, leave review feedback, mention teammates, and resolve conversations near the proposed change.
employeeUseCase: A developer reviewing a merge request can comment on the overview or on changed lines, reply in a thread, mention teammates with @username, and resolve discussions after the feedback is handled.
highlights: Comments and discussions keep review feedback close to the merge request context.
Reviewers can comment on specific lines or files in a merge request diff.
Threads help separate different questions or feedback items during review.
Resolved discussions show which feedback has been addressed before merge.

title: CI/CD and Verify
summary: GitLab CI/CD and Verify help teams automate tests, get fast feedback, and reduce delivery risk before software reaches users.
employeeUseCase: Engineering candidates can explain CI/CD as a feedback system: it catches issues earlier, supports quality, and helps teams ship with more confidence.
highlights: Fast CI feedback helps developers correct problems while context is fresh.
Automation reduces dependence on manual release checks.
Verify connects quality signals to the larger DevSecOps lifecycle.

title: Security and Governance
summary: GitLab security direction focuses on integrating security into developer workflows so teams can identify, prioritize, and remediate risks earlier.
employeeUseCase: Security and engineering teams can frame secure development as part of normal delivery, not as a disconnected final gate.
highlights: Security is more effective when developers can see and fix risks inside their workflow.
Prioritization matters because teams need to know which vulnerabilities deserve attention first.
Governance and visibility help organizations manage risk across the software lifecycle.

title: Planning and Prioritization
summary: GitLab planning connects strategy to execution through visible priorities, issues, ownership, and tradeoff documentation.
employeeUseCase: Product and engineering employees can use planning artifacts to show why a priority matters and how it connects to customer value.
highlights: Visible planning artifacts reduce hidden context and make tradeoffs easier to inspect.
Issues and portfolio planning connect strategy to day-to-day work.
Prioritization is stronger when customer value and ownership are explicit.

title: Issues and Work Items
summary: Yes. In GitLab, the closest product concept to raising a ticket is creating an issue or work item in a project to track tasks, bugs, feature proposals, support requests, or planned work.
employeeUseCase: A new GitLab user should usually think 'create an issue' rather than 'raise a ticket'; issues belong to projects and can be discussed, assigned, labeled, prioritized, and tracked on boards.
highlights: GitLab issues help teams plan, track, discuss, and deliver work.
Issues can track feature proposals, tasks, support requests, and bug reports.
Users can create issues from projects, groups, existing issues, issue boards, email, URLs with prefilled values, or Service Desk.
Creating issues requires access to the relevant project, such as Guest, Planner, Reporter, Developer, Maintainer, or Owner permissions.

title: GitLab Direction
summary: GitLab's product process guidance treats Direction pages as a critical way to communicate where product areas are heading and why.
employeeUseCase: Employees and candidates can use Direction pages to understand how individual features connect to GitLab's broader product strategy.
highlights: Direction pages communicate where GitLab is investing and how product areas evolve.
The public direction format invites customers, contributors, candidates, and team members to understand priorities.
Product direction connects individual categories to the broader DevSecOps platform strategy.

title: DevSecOps Platform
summary: GitLab positions itself around a comprehensive DevSecOps platform that supports planning, source code, CI/CD, security, observability, and collaboration across the software lifecycle.
employeeUseCase: Product and engineering employees can explain decisions in terms of reducing handoffs between development, security, and operations.
highlights: A single platform can reduce handoffs across development, security, and operations teams.
The product strategy focuses on connecting stages of the software delivery lifecycle.
Direction content helps employees understand customer workflows and category priorities.

title: AI-Powered DevSecOps
summary: GitLab's direction increasingly frames AI as a way to improve productivity, security, and software delivery across the DevSecOps lifecycle.
employeeUseCase: Candidates can stand out by discussing AI as workflow augmentation across planning, coding, review, security, and operations rather than a single chatbot feature.
highlights: AI features are strongest when they are grounded in the software delivery workflow.
AI should reduce friction across DevSecOps stages instead of creating another disconnected tool.
Responsible AI direction should preserve trust, security, and source visibility.

title: GitLab Duo
summary: GitLab Duo represents GitLab's AI capabilities for helping teams write, review, secure, and understand software inside the DevSecOps workflow.
employeeUseCase: A product-minded answer can describe GitLab Duo as AI embedded into developer workflows with security and governance expectations.
highlights: GitLab Duo is most relevant when the user asks about AI in GitLab's product direction.
AI assistance should be evaluated by workflow impact, not novelty alone.
Trust and source context matter when AI is used for engineering and security work.

title: Secure Stage Direction
summary: the Secure stage direction focuses on helping teams identify, prioritize, and remediate security risks within the software delivery lifecycle.
employeeUseCase: Employees can connect security features to the broader DevSecOps strategy by explaining how security shifts earlier and becomes part of normal delivery.
highlights: Security is stronger when it is integrated into developer workflows.
Prioritization and remediation matter as much as detecting vulnerabilities.
Secure direction connects security work with platform-level visibility and governance.

title: Verify Stage Direction
summary: the Verify stage direction covers CI, testing, quality signals, and automation that help teams ship software with confidence.
employeeUseCase: Engineering candidates can tie CI/CD questions to reliability, feedback speed, and reducing delivery risk.
highlights: Fast feedback loops help teams catch problems earlier.
CI and testing are central parts of the DevSecOps lifecycle.
Automation supports consistent quality without relying only on manual review.

title: Plan Stage Direction
summary: the Plan stage direction focuses on portfolio planning, issue workflows, product management, and connecting strategy to execution.
employeeUseCase: Product candidates can connect planning features to transparency, prioritization, and reducing handoffs before implementation begins.
highlights: Planning work is more effective when priorities and tradeoffs are visible.
Issues and planning artifacts create shared context for distributed teams.
Plan direction connects strategy with the execution work that follows.

title: Create and Source Code Direction
summary: GitLab's Create and source code direction concerns code review, repository workflows, developer experience, and collaboration around changes.
employeeUseCase: Engineers can frame merge requests as both implementation artifacts and collaboration spaces for transparent review.
highlights: Code review is a collaboration mechanism, not only a quality gate.
Repository workflows connect planning, implementation, review, and delivery.
Developer experience improves when context stays close to the change.
